subject: Question regarding data aggregation for a CPF species

messages.author: 5b54e1085854c480
messages.subject: Question regarding data aggregation for a CPF species
parts:
Dear all, 

I am working on a central-place foraging species and have a dataset of a few thousand tracks.

I am investigating the presence of segregation among the colony's home range. I am then modelling the spatial distribution at the individual-level, for thereafter testing segregation by randomization procedure using the overlap() function (i.e. over colony affiliation of the individuals).

Individual tracking was first segmented into foraging trips, in order to reduce the weight of the numerous localization at the colony between the foraging trips. Since the overlap() function doesn't appear to be reliable when implemented with the average distributions (e.g. from mean.UD), I am searching for the most optimal way of aggregating data within the individual stratum. So far, I am considering continuous time between each individual's trip, and by removing the "extra" localisation at the colony (i.e. except the departure and arrival points to the colony). In other words, we have a regular interval of 10 min between every two locations within individuals, having thus a maximum of 10 min at the colony before the next trip.

By doing so, and since periodicity is low in the data, the ctmm.fit() give sensible results. However, I am curious to know if another (proper?) way is existing for dealing with such data?

Furthermore, I have noticed that sometimes the variograms doesn't show all the lags, although numbers occur in the input data frame. I suspect a DOF effect since that one is < 1 (according to https://rdrr.io/cran/ctmm/src/R/variogram.R). However, would the estimates from such structure be reliable?


Many thanks again, best /Phil

messages.author: 40fd627580dd34f5
messages.subject: Re: Question regarding data aggregation for a CPF species
parts:
Hi Phil,

  1. Proper CIs on mean UDs are in the short-term pipeline, but I don't know what time constraints you have, so don't wait for me.
  2. ctmm is currently limited to stationary processes (with the simple exception of non-stationary mean functions), and that will be a longer-term upgrade. So it is a good idea to segment the data into individual behaviors before fitting a stationary model. If I understand what you are doing correctly, there does not need to be a maximum threshold of time between trips. You just want to have the nesting behavior removed.
  3. If you change the fraction argument of plot.variogram, it can show all of the lags. Alternatively, you can use the slider in zoom().
Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Re: Question regarding data aggregation for a CPF species
parts:
Hi Chris, 

This thread is a bit old but would be curious to get some precision on one of your previous comment (July 1st 2020).

For summarizing the original background: I am working on a central-place foraging species, which under chick-rearing comes back and forth to its colony, roughly every ~ 4 hours. While computing individual-level home range estimates (via AKDE), I wanted to minimize the "colony weight" in order to focus on the "foraging behavior", meaning focusing only on locations outside the colony.

For doing so, I have removed all colony locations, except the first and the last points of each (complete) trip. Within trips, all locations are separated by a standard interval of 10 minutes. Since each individual has many trips (~ 4 trips/individual), I reshaped the timespan of each individual tracking period, having thus a 10 minutes interval between every individual's trip, resulting in a maximum time spent at the colony of 10 minutes. This approach was firstly intended to avoid large time gaps (~ 4-6 hours) between trips. By doing so, however, I was also changing the natural timespan of the tracking period, which ultimately was also affecting the estimates from the autocorrelation function.

On this approach, you stated previously:

1. ctmm is currently limited to stationary processes (with the simple exception of non-stationary mean functions), and that will be a longer-term upgrade. So it is a good idea to segment the data into individual behaviors before fitting a stationary model. If I understand what you are doing correctly, there does not need to be a maximum threshold of time between trips. You just want to have the nesting behavior removed.

By reading your comment again, I am now considering changing my approach: by simply removing all colony points (thus focusing on points outside the colony) while keeping the natural timespan between all locations. Doing so, however, will generate gaps of many hours during the tracking period (equivalent to the time spent at the colony). But as read in your paper (2018, Ecological Applications 28), the AKDE could deal with such missing locations.

My question: Would you recommend to consider using the original timespan of the tracking period while removing the locations from the colony, despite the imposed cyclical gaps in GPS location? 

Hopefully, this thread could help other users dealing with CPF-based data. Thank you again for your ongoing help. /Phil

messages.author: 40fd627580dd34f5
messages.subject: Re: Question regarding data aggregation for a CPF species
parts:
Hi Philip,

Yes, I don't think you need a maximum threshold of time between trips because the start and end points are both at the nest. In a completely different situation where you have segmented behaviors and those points are far apart, then you might want to dilate the time between to prevent long-ranged correlation.

If you plan to turn weights on in AKDE, then I would actually reduce the time between trips to the sampling interval, to avoid placing large weights on the colonies. But I would only worry about weights if the foraging period suffers irregular sampling.

Best,
Chris
